idiom_name: scala.concurrent.Future + Promise with an implicit ExecutionContext
implementation_notes: The standard library ships both ends: a Future is a placeholder object for a value that may not yet exist whose value is supplied concurrently, and a Promise is the object to complete with a value or fail with an exception - the documentation states that it should always eventually be completed, or the associated futures retain their callbacks. Composition is non-blocking by default through map/flatMap/filter/foreach, so callbacks are replaced by combinators, and each of them needs an implicit ExecutionContext as the scheduler; blocking via Await.result is possible but explicitly discouraged, and Scala 3 keeps the same API.
code_sketch:
implicit val ec: ExecutionContext = ExecutionContext.global
val p = Promise[Summary]()                       // write end (single assignment)
val f: Future[Summary] = p.future                // read end
val sizes = f.map(_.size).recover { case _: TimeoutException => 0 }
p.success(compute())            // resolve once; failures go through p.failure(e)
pitfalls: Combinators run on whatever ExecutionContext is implicitly in scope: blocking calls or CPU-heavy work on the global pool starves unrelated futures, so give blocking work its own bounded pool.

Waiting with Await.result inside a callback that runs on the same small pool is the classic deadlock (and the reason the documentation discourages blocking) - keep composition non-blocking and block only at the program's edge.
An uncompleted Promise keeps the callbacks and transformations of its futures alive, and settling it twice is rejected by the API: resolve exactly once, on every exit path.
